🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -0.62% (intraday, 7-year +9bp). At trading day 41 (last close) it was -0.60% against a five-campaign average of -1.48% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.63%. The 10-year is +11bp since the hike vs a +18bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 3 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 780bp against a five-year average of 420bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is holding: single-B -10bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.33 → 0.65 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.69). Investment grade is untouched (+3bp).
  • AI Credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS 1,076bp, -88bp since 2026-11-12, 119bp under the Oct 15 record and 624bp over the June low. Its June 9.625% 2032s are at 82.0 (14.4%, +4.1pts in a month). Up the stack: Nvidia 142bp, Oracle 300bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -14%, NBIS -31%, IREN -36% vs NVDA -25%.
  • Tech Phase: Phase 1 of the 2000 template, day 28 after the tech basket's 2026-10-06 peak: basket -16.7% vs -16.5% for 2000 on the same day. Model odds of being in spread widening or worse: 34% in 3m, 31% in 6m; odds spreads cross the Phase-2 line at some point within 12m: 50%. 6m odds -6.1pp since 2026-11-12. Triggered signposts: Basket names >20% off high; SOX.

Friday's tape repeated the month's main story: tech was sold and defensives were bought. The Nasdaq Composite fell -0.91% to 25,136.27 and the S&P 500 fell -0.40% to 7,561.67, while the Dow rose +0.10% to 52,347.55. US Info Tech lost -1.70% on the day and is -9.36% over the month. Consumer Staples (+1.39%), Energy (+0.96%) and Financials (+0.80%) led. The VIX rose 0.6 to 19.3. Technically the Nasdaq now sits exactly on its 200-day average (computed distance -0.0%) and is -4.61% below its 50-day. Rates bull-steepened at the front end: the 2Y fell 3.95bp to 4.8419% while the 10Y (5.1352%) and 30Y (5.4655%) rose. Long ends rose globally too: JGB 10Y +5.8bp to 2.871%, Gilt +3.6bp, Bund +3bp. Credit is the important nuance. Broad spreads are calm: IG OAS was unchanged at 86bp and HY widened only 4bp to 316bp. But the computed HY contagion panel shows the Caa–B gap at 780bp against a 236bp-wider... (5y average 420bp), in the 99th percentile of 5 years (pctl5y 99.2), +48bp over 1m and +205bp over 3m. FRED's CCC–B cross-check is 983bp (pctl5y 99.1). Is the CCC stress spreading? So far, mostly no. Single-B (303bp, -10bp 1m) and BB (181bp, -15bp 1m) both tightened over the month, and the B–Ba gap of 122bp sits near its 5y average of 128.8bp. The 63-day Caa/B correlation has risen to 0.65 from 0.33 three months ago, though it remains below its 5y median of 0.69. That rise is the thing to watch. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. The AI-credit backstop question got a constructive week. CoreWeave 5Y CDS fell 88.5bp on the day and 237.3bp on the week to 1,075.9bp. That is 118.6bp below the 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record, but it still retains 84% of the run from the 452bp June low. Nvidia CDS eased 2.11bp to 141.69bp. CoreWeave's notes are up about 5–6.5 points since their Nov 5 lows, and CRWV stock rose 29.6% on the week. The market is partly buying Nvidia's backstop of the neoclouds, but only partly: CoreWeave CDS is still near record territory and Nvidia's DRSK model-implied CDS is at its 1-year high (100th percentile). Descriptive only. The tech-analog phase model still places the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 28 days from the peak. The basket drawdown is -16.66%, versus -16.52% for the 2000 basket on the same day. Two signposts are triggered. Breadth: 57.1% of basket names are more than 20% off their highs (trigger 50%). SOX: -30.67% from its 52-week high (trigger -30%). The model's 6m Phase-2/3 odds fell 6.1pp from Thursday, and the 12m ever-Phase-2+ odds fell 5.6pp. Sentiment reads cautious, not panicked: AAII bull-bear is -20.6 and credit regimes are 96.6% 'calm'.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 425.85 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is trading at 425.85 cents/gal, near the top of its history on every measure here: outright price (99.1 pctile), the crack spread (99.3 pctile) and all three curve spreads (96.4 to 98.0 pctile). The curve is steeply backwardated, falling from 425.85 at the front to 341.25 at month 12 and 263.85 at month 36. That shape points to a squeeze on prompt barrels and unusually strong refining margins, not to a lasting reset higher in diesel prices. Every card gives a SELL signal, but the stops are very wide. Fading the extreme makes sense, but sizing has to allow for further spikes while the squeeze lasts.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.75 vol points (54th percentile of the 68 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 98.8 (71th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 90bp (steeper by 0bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

Cup window fixed at 2000-present; swing detection uses a +/-6-week window on closes; cup pass = >= 90% retracement of the left-rim decline; ascending-triangle pass = slope>0, p<0.05, and >=60% of swing-low steps higher. This is pattern analysis of historical price data, not investment advice, and nothing here forecasts a level or a direction.

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 43 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 62/100 — Underlying inflation is moderately persistent, not accelerating sharply. Every trimmed and median measure sits above 2%, and the sticky components are rising. The computed Core-Trend Sub-Score is shown separately. Breadth is mixed: the Dallas distribution has 16.6% of the PCE basket running above 10% and 10.2% at 5–10%, but 25.6% is falling. Markets are not pricing persistence: the 1y breakeven is 2.0727% and the 5y is 2.3047%, both below the realized core figures. That gap is a risk if sticky inflation holds into 2027.

The computed indicators show: - Nasdaq trailing P/E 39x vs the 175x peak (15% of the way) - Nasdaq stretch vs its 200DMA 0% - SOX P/E 34.37x (36%) Catalyst and regime conditions are past 2000 levels: - IG spread tightness 128% and Baa–10Y tightness 175% of the 2000 condition - NFCI financial conditions 148% - Commodities-vs-equities 200% - VIX complacency 155% Sentiment is not euphoric: AAII bull–bear is at 0% of the 2000 condition and consumer confidence at 31%. The phase model puts the tech basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm). The basket drawdown is -16.66%, nearly identical to the 2000 basket's -16.52% on the same day. The model estimates, at 6m: Phase 1 57.8%, Phase 2 17.8%, Phase 3 13.4%, Phase 4 11.0%. It estimates a 50.1% chance of ever reaching Phase 2+ within 12m. Two signposts have triggered: breadth (57.1% of names more than 20% off their highs) and SOX (-30.67% from its high). The 6m Phase-2/3 odds fell 6.1pp from the prior session. In short, this looks like 2000's early drawdown in price, not in valuation, and credit has not confirmed.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analog is a price-path match, not a valuation match. Today's tech leaders trade at a fraction of 2000 multiples. The computed late-cycle backdrop, though, is as easy as or easier than 2000: very tight credit, loose financial conditions and a low VIX. That is why the phase model still gives meaningful odds of a credit-confirmed Phase 2 over 12–24 months. The rally watch shows credit calm is in place (HY -24bp over 10 days). The VIX spike-and-turn conditions are not, and the model gives only 9.3% odds that the conditions align within 10 days. Historically 44.1% of such rallies were traps. The concentration, IPO-froth, CAPE, Buffett-ratio and long-term EPS-growth figures in this section are analyst estimates, not verified this session; treat them as approximate. The most anticipated IPO, Anthropic, is reportedly meeting a weaker tech tape than it expected, which argues against 2000-style IPO mania.

Odds the volatility-washout conditions line up within a week: 4%; within two weeks: 9%. Rallies of 8%+ that start in this phase: 44% later fail below their starting low (median 13 trading days, +10%); the rest become recoveries (median 86 days, +31%). Descriptive, not a signal.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at the Dec 8–9 FOMC. This is an inference. Warsh has said on record that he won't prejudge meetings for the rest of 2026 and named October and December as the decision points. The committee followed a September hike with restrictive-for-longer language, and core PCE is 3.12%. The 2Y falling to 4.8419% suggests markets are leaning toward no further hikes.

~1 YEAR

Inferred, not stated by Warsh: a gradual shift toward cuts in 2027 if core inflation rolls over and the labor market softens. Some analysts cited see 25bp cuts possible at the December 2026 and March 2027 meetings, but the Fed's spring wording pointed the other way. Our inference from Warsh's long-standing public positions, not re-verified this session, is a preference for less forward guidance and a smaller balance sheet. That could mean any rate cuts come paired with balance-sheet restraint, which supports the front end more than the long end.

The verified record is thin and partly dated. Warsh refuses to give forward guidance on the remaining 2026 meetings (investinglive). Earlier coverage described him inheriting a hawkish, divided FOMC as cut hopes faded on the Iran war: the April minutes dropped 'nimble' language, and three reserve-bank presidents dissented against language implying the next move would be a cut (investinglive, Sinclair/KATV). I could not confirm the October meeting outcome or the current target range, so the policy-rate level is n/a here. The near-term and 1-year calls above are inferences from the cited material plus current data, not stated Warsh plans.
